# 056 · A lookupswitch pair sort that compares keys by difference

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: counterexample found** | functional | high | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`SwitchLowering#sortPairs`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/asm/SwitchLowering.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../lib/README.md) |

> The assembler sorts the match-offset pairs of a `lookupswitch` by key, as JVMS §6.5 requires, with an insertion sort that keeps each offset with its key. A developer factors the comparison into a `compare` method that returns the difference of the two keys, the comparator idiom. The property committed for the sort says that the keys come out sorted and that every pair the call received is among the pairs it left, in JML's `\old`. The prover refutes the patched sort on two keys in order whose difference overflows, `Integer.MIN_VALUE + 271` and `272`, which it swaps.

Tags: [jvm-internals](../README.md#tag-jvm-internals), [compilers](../README.md#tag-compilers), [array-utilities](../README.md#tag-array-utilities), [integer-overflow](../README.md#tag-integer-overflow), [jml-quantifiers](../README.md#tag-jml-quantifiers), [jml-old](../README.md#tag-jml-old), [throws-clause](../README.md#tag-throws-clause)

## The change

Replace `keys[j - 1] > key` in the inner loop with `compare(keys[j - 1], key) > 0`, where the new `compare` returns `a - b`, documented as a comparator's result: negative, zero or positive. The tests of the sort pass: three pairs in reverse order, three in order, and a table with a missing offset.

**Before** ([`SwitchLowering.java`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/asm/SwitchLowering.java), line 44):

```java
            int key = keys[i];
            int offset = offsets[i];
            int j = i;
            while (j > 0 && keys[j - 1] > key) {
                keys[j] = keys[j - 1];
                offsets[j] = offsets[j - 1];
                j--;
    // ...
            offsets[j] = offset;
        }
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
            int key = keys[i];
            int offset = offsets[i];
            int j = i;
            while (j > 0 && compare(keys[j - 1], key) > 0) {
                keys[j] = keys[j - 1];
                offsets[j] = offsets[j - 1];
                j--;
    // ...
            offsets[j] = offset;
        }
    }

    /** The order of two case labels: negative, zero or positive, as a comparator's. */
    static int compare(int a, int b) {
        return a - b;
    }
}
```

```diff
--- a/examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/asm/SwitchLowering.java
+++ b/examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/asm/SwitchLowering.java
@@ -44,7 +44,7 @@
             int key = keys[i];
             int offset = offsets[i];
             int j = i;
-            while (j > 0 && keys[j - 1] > key) {
+            while (j > 0 && compare(keys[j - 1], key) > 0) {
                 keys[j] = keys[j - 1];
                 offsets[j] = offsets[j - 1];
                 j--;
@@ -53,4 +53,9 @@
             offsets[j] = offset;
         }
     }
+
+    /** The order of two case labels: negative, zero or positive, as a comparator's. */
+    static int compare(int a, int b) {
+        return a - b;
+    }
```

## What the verifier found

The property does not hold: that `(\forall int i; 0 < i && i < keys.length; keys[i - 1] <= keys[i]) && (\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < keys.length; (\exists int j; 0 <= j && j < keys.length; keys[j] == \old(keys[i]) && offsets[j] == \old(offsets[i])))` holds on every input, and throws `java.lang.IllegalArgumentException` exactly when `keys.length != offsets.length`. The prover found this input, and the tool replayed it on the method to show what it does:

| Input | The method's outcome |
|---|---|
| `sortPairs(keys=[-2147483377, 272], offsets=[0, 0])` | `void, leaving keys=[272, -2147483377]` |

One input is enough to fail the build. The domain is `keys: int[] of length ≤ 4 × offsets: int[] of length ≤ 4`; the search tries small values first so that the witness is readable, and would have covered all of it.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

`a - b` is the sign of `a` compared with `b` only when the subtraction does not overflow, and the case labels of a `switch` are any `int`: a `switch` on a hash code, or on `Integer.MIN_VALUE` as a sentinel, has labels whose difference wraps. A pair the sort leaves out of order is a table the `lookupswitch` bisection searches wrongly: the key is in the table and the search returns the default, so the guest program takes the wrong branch, with no exception and no diagnostic, on a class file that passes verification. The tests use labels between 10 and 300.

## Why the verdict is right

The property committed for `sortPairs` is two quantifiers: `(\forall int i; 0 < i && i < keys.length; keys[i - 1] <= keys[i])`, the keys are sorted, and `(\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < keys.length; (\exists int j; 0 <= j && j < keys.length; keys[j] == \old(keys[i]) && offsets[j] == \old(offsets[i])))`, every pair as the call received it is among the pairs after it, which with the lengths equal makes the sort a permutation that keeps each offset with its key. `\old` is JML's pre-state operator; the tool copies the arrays in the generated harness before the call and reads the copies under it. The block also sets `arrays: 4` and `unwind: 5`: a sort of four pairs and the pairing quantifier are both quadratic, and the proof of the committed sort takes about fifteen seconds with the loops unwound five times, where the default of sixteen takes minutes. JBMC refutes the patched sort in the first search stage, and the tool shrinks the witness to `sortPairs(keys=[-2147483377, 272], offsets=[0, 0])`: two keys already in order, `Integer.MIN_VALUE + 271` and `272`, whose difference is `-2147483649`, which wraps to `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, positive, so the sort shifts the first past the second and leaves `keys=[272, -2147483377]`, and the sortedness conjunct fails. The witness is a table of two keys just over `2^31` apart, the smallest distance at which a comparator by difference lies; the shrinking stops there because any smaller distance is a difference that fits.

## What to do

Revert to the comparison, or make `compare` return `Integer.compare(a, b)`, and keep the property in the build: it is the test that `compare` on every pair of `int` labels is a total order, which no table of sample labels is.

## Notes

- Comparing keys by difference overflows and swaps two keys just over 2^31 apart, refuted against a permutation stated with JML's `\old`.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: found by JBMC 6.11.0 in 0.7 s searching inputs in [0:20] as sortPairs(keys=[1041, -2147483648, 1, 272], offsets=[-1091355143, -1091355143, -1944199553, -474718690]), shrunk to the input above in 389 interpreter runs, replayed in the interpreter; domain keys: int[] of length ≤ 4 × offsets: int[] of length ≤ 4.

```java
/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts a property of a method on every input. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
/* \forall, \exists, \sum, \num_of, \max and \min are JML's quantifiers; the class file evaluates each as a loop over its range. */
/* \old(a) is the array a as it was before the call: the class file copies it first. */
public final class PropertyHarness {
    public static void check(int[] keys, int[] offsets) {
        int e = 0;
        int expected = 0; // the throws clause that applies: the first whose condition holds
        if (keys.length != offsets.length) { expected = 1; } // java.lang.IllegalArgumentException
        try { net.terminalvalue.mica.asm.SwitchLowering.sortPairs(keys, offsets); } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { e = -1; } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { e = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { e = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { e = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { e = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { e = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { e = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { e = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { e = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { e = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { e = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { e = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { e = 15; }
        assert expected != 0 ? e == -expected : e == 0 && ((\forall int i; 0 < i && i < keys.length; keys[i - 1] <= keys[i]) && (\forall int i; 0 <= i && i < keys.length; (\exists int j; 0 <= j && j < keys.length; keys[j] == \old(keys[i]) && offsets[j] == \old(offsets[i])))); // the declared exception where its condition holds; elsewhere no exception, and the property
    }
}
```

**Provenance:** Constructed from the comparator-by-difference idiom, which Java's own `Integer.compare` exists to replace, applied to the sort an assembler needs for JVMS §6.5.

- [JVMS §6.5, lookupswitch: the match-offset pairs must be sorted in increasing numerical order by match](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jvms/se21/html/jvms-6.html#jvms-6.5.lookupswitch)
- [Integer.compare: the comparison the difference idiom gets wrong on overflow](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Integer.html#compare(int,int))
- [JML reference manual, predicates and specification expressions: \old, the value of an expression in the pre-state](https://www.cs.ucf.edu/~leavens/JML/jmlrefman/jmlrefman_11.html)
